clinicalPearls: Classic presentation is chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea in an older adult (often 60s-70s) with a grossly and endoscopically normal-appearing colon
Female predominance is marked, especially for the collagenous subtype
Strongly associated with NSAID use, proton pump inhibitors, SSRIs, and statins — a careful drug history is essential
Frequently coexists with autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, and other connective tissue or rheumatologic disorders
Diagnosis requires random biopsies from multiple colonic segments even when mucosa looks endoscopically normal, since gross findings are typically absent
Two histologic subtypes — collagenous (thickened subepithelial collagen band) and lymphocytic (increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) — share similar clinical behavior and management
Nocturnal diarrhea and fecal urgency/incontinence are common and can significantly impair quality of life despite the benign histology
Weight loss and abdominal pain can occur but are typically milder than in classic inflammatory bowel disease
harrison.pathophysiology: Microscopic colitis is thought to result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens (including bile acids, bacterial products, and certain drugs) in a genetically or immunologically susceptible host, producing intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration with or without subepithelial collagen deposition. This impairs colonic epithelial barrier function and fluid/electrolyte absorption, producing a secretory-type watery diarrhea without gross mucosal ulceration. The strong drug and autoimmune associations support an immune-mediated rather than structural mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis)
Drug-induced diarrhea (independent of microscopic colitis itself)
nonInfectiousMimics: Endocrine causes of diarrhea (e.g., hyperthyroidism, neuroendocrine tumors)
additionalInvestigations: Colonoscopy with random biopsies from multiple colonic segments — required for histologic diagnosis since mucosa often appears normal
Histopathology — distinguishes collagenous (thickened collagen band) from lymphocytic (intraepithelial lymphocytosis) subtype
Celiac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) — screens for coexisting celiac disease
Thyroid function tests — screens for associated autoimmune thyroid disease
Stool studies (culture, C. difficile testing, ova and parasites) — excludes infectious causes of chronic diarrhea
Medication review — identifies causative drugs such as NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, and statins
Fecal calprotectin — typically normal or only mildly elevated, helps differentiate from classic IBD
SeHCAT or serum C4/FGF-19 testing where available — evaluates for concurrent bile acid diarrhea
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, anemia, or weight loss suggesting an alternative or coexisting diagnosis rather than uncomplicated microscopic colitis
Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhea
Failure to respond to standard therapy — warrants reassessment for IBD, celiac disease, or bile acid diarrhea
New abdominal pain, fever, or peritoneal signs, which are atypical and require evaluation for another process
Persistent symptoms despite discontinuation of an implicated drug
pitfalls: Assuming a normal-appearing colonoscopy excludes colitis — biopsies are mandatory since gross findings are usually absent
Failing to obtain biopsies from multiple segments, as histologic changes can be patchy or segment-specific
Overlooking a causative medication and treating chronically without attempting drug discontinuation
Missing coexisting celiac disease or bile acid diarrhea, which can perpetuate symptoms despite colitis-directed therapy
harrison.prognosis: Microscopic colitis is a benign, non-progressive condition that does not increase colorectal cancer risk and often responds well to drug withdrawal or medical therapy, though relapses are common after treatment discontinuation and a subset of patients follow a chronic intermittent course.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Inflammatory Bowel Disease and related colitides (Gastroenterology section, diarrhea and colitis topics)
management: Withdraw implicated drugs — NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, SSRIs, and statins — as a first step
Induce remission with oral budesonide, the most effective agent, and use it for maintenance in relapsing disease at the lowest effective dose
Control mild symptoms with antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide, adding a bile acid sequestrant like cholestyramine where bile acid malabsorption contributes
For budesonide-refractory or -dependent disease, consider immunomodulators or anti-TNF biologics, reserving surgery for rare severe cases
Screen for and manage coexisting autoimmune conditions, particularly coeliac disease and autoimmune thyroid disease
Reassure regarding the benign, non-neoplastic course while anticipating and re-treating relapses
